triples.relationship: named royal commission and narrative counterpart
triples.rationale: Isaiah names Cyrus as the ruler whose hand God grasps to subdue nations. Ezra names Cyrus, attributes his kingdoms and Jerusalem commission to the Lord, and records the proclamation enabling the return. Ezra does not repeat the anointing language.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord God to My anointed Cyrus, whose right hand I grasped so that nations would heed him: “I will shatter kings’ strength, open doors before him, and cities will not be shut.

target_units.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, so that the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians. He ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom, also in writing, saying:
“Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord, God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judea.
Who among you belongs to any of His people? His God will be with him, and he will go up to Jerusalem in Judea. Let him build the house of the God of Israel—He is the God in Jerusalem.

As for everyone left behind, from whatever place he resides in, the men of his place will take him up with silver, gold, belongings and livestock, together with the freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem.”

triples.relationship: close verbal parallel in shattered barriers
triples.rationale: Both attribute the shattering of bronze gates or doors and the breaking of iron bars to God. Isaiah applies the imagery to the way opened before Cyrus; the psalm praises divine deliverance.
triples.source_text: I will go before you and level mountains. I will shatter bronze doors and break iron bars.

target_units.text: Let them acknowledge to the Lord His mercies and His wonders to the sons of men,
for He shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars.

triples.relationship: internal divine calling by name
triples.rationale: The God who calls Cyrus by name in Isaiah 45 also tells Jacob and Israel that He called them by name in Isaiah 43. The recipients differ; the repeated personal summons belongs to the same God's purposeful action.
triples.source_text: I will give you dark treasures and open hidden, unseen stores to you, so that you may know that I am the Lord God who calls your name, Israel’s God.

target_units.text: But now thus says the Lord God who made you, Jacob, who formed you, Israel: “Do not fear, for I redeemed you. I called you by your name; you are Mine.

triples.relationship: internal identification of the chosen servant
triples.rationale: Isaiah 45 explains Cyrus's call by reference to God's servant Jacob and chosen Israel. Isaiah 41 explicitly calls Israel and Jacob God's chosen servant and describes taking and calling that servant.
triples.source_text: For the sake of My servant Jacob and Israel My chosen one, I will call you by your name and welcome you; yet you did not know Me.

target_units.text: But you, Israel, My servant Jacob whom I chose, offspring of Abraham whom I loved,
whom I took hold of from the earth’s extremities, and from its lookout heights called you and said, ‘You are My servant; I chose you and did not abandon you’—

triples.relationship: shared declaration of divine uniqueness
triples.rationale: Isaiah declares that the Lord is God with none besides Him, despite Cyrus's lack of knowledge. Deuteronomy uses the same exclusive declaration as the knowledge Israel should gain from God's acts.
triples.source_text: For I am the Lord God, and there is no god besides Me, and you did not know Me,

to destroy nations great and mightier than you from before you, to bring you in, and to give you their land to inherit, as you have this day.

triples.relationship: shared worldwide recognition from sunrise to sunset
triples.rationale: Both use the span from the sun's rising to its setting for recognition of the Lord among peoples. Isaiah emphasizes knowing there is no other God; Malachi emphasizes His glorified name and worship.
triples.source_text: so that those from the sun’s rising and those from its setting may know that there is none besides Me. I am the Lord God, and there is no other.

triples.relationship: divine agency in calamity
triples.rationale: Isaiah expressly says that God makes peace and creates calamities. Amos similarly asks whether a calamity occurs in a city without the Lord doing it. Neither connection requires replacing calamities with a claim that God commits moral wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: I fashioned light and made darkness; I make peace and create calamities. I am the Lord God, who does all these things.

target_units.text: Will a trumpet sound in a city and the people not be alarmed? Will there be calamity in a city that the Lord has not done?

triples.relationship: creation of light and ordering of darkness
triples.rationale: Isaiah identifies God as the One fashioning light and making darkness. Genesis narrates God's command bringing light and His division and naming of light and darkness within creation.
triples.source_text: I fashioned light and made darkness; I make peace and create calamities. I am the Lord God, who does all these things.

target_units.text: In the beginning God made heaven and earth.

And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening, and there was morning: one day.

triples.relationship: shared heavenly and earthly growth imagery
triples.rationale: Isaiah calls clouds to sprinkle righteousness and earth to produce mercy and righteousness. The psalm likewise joins mercy and righteousness with truth springing from earth, righteousness looking from heaven, and the land yielding fruit.

triples.relationship: creation of earth and the heavenly array
triples.rationale: Isaiah attributes earth, its humanity, heaven and the commanded stars to God's hand. Nehemiah's prayer likewise names the Lord alone as maker of heaven and its array, earth and everything in it.
triples.source_text: I made earth and humanity upon it. With My hand I established heaven; I commanded all the stars.

triples.source_text: for Thou art God, and we did not know it, Israel’s God, the Savior.’”

triples.rationale: Isaiah 45 says God's opponents will be ashamed and abashed. Isaiah 41 uses the same paired shame language for those opposing His people; the stated objects of opposition differ.
triples.source_text: All who oppose Him will be ashamed and abashed and go away in shame. “Be renewed toward Me, islands.”

triples.relationship: Israel's salvation and enduring divine commitment
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises Israel salvation by the Lord without final shame. Romans also speaks of Israel being saved, relating that hope to the Deliverer and God's covenant taking away sins; it develops a distinct argument concerning Gentiles and Israel.
triples.source_text: Israel is saved by the Lord with everlasting salvation. They will not be ashamed or ever be abashed for eternity.

And this is My covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”

triples.relationship: open speech contrasted with secrecy
triples.rationale: The Lord in Isaiah denies speaking secretly or in a dark place. Jesus in John's account likewise says He spoke openly and nothing in secret, directing questioners to His hearers. This compares the explicit public-speech claims without equating their immediate settings.

triples.rationale: Isaiah exposes people carrying a wooden image and praying to gods unable to save. Jeremiah describes wooden manufactured gods that must be carried because they cannot move and have no good in them.

triples.relationship: internal challenge of prediction and unique salvation
triples.rationale: Both passages challenge other claimants to announce what was known from the beginning, then declare the Lord's unique identity and saving power. The combination of announcement, witnesses or assembled hearers, and exclusive salvation grounds the connection.

triples.rationale: Isaiah calls people at the earth's extremity to turn to God and be saved. Acts rejects manufactured divinity and commands all people everywhere to repent, adding the appointed judgment through the risen Man.

Therefore, having overlooked the times of ignorance, God now commands all people everywhere to repent,
because He has fixed a day on which He will judge the inhabited world in righteousness through a Man whom He appointed, giving assurance to everyone by raising Him from the dead.”

triples.rationale: Romans introduces as written the declaration that every knee will bend and every tongue confess to God, matching Isaiah's central wording. Paul uses it to explain each person's accountability at God's judgment seat.
triples.source_text: By Myself I swear: Surely righteousness will go out from My mouth; My words will not return, because every knee will bend to Me and every tongue will confess to God,

for it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bend to Me, and every tongue will confess to God.”
So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.

triples.relationship: New Testament reuse of universal homage language
triples.rationale: Philippians repeats the bending of every knee and confession of every tongue in its account of Jesus's exaltation. Isaiah's universal homage to God supplies the corresponding wording; Philippians explicitly names Jesus Christ as Lord and God the Father as glorified.
triples.source_text: By Myself I swear: Surely righteousness will go out from My mouth; My words will not return, because every knee will bend to Me and every tongue will confess to God,

so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth,
and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 45 sets righteousness and glory coming to Him beside shame for those setting themselves apart. Isaiah 41 likewise announces shame and disappearance for adversaries. and those whom He predestined, these He also called; and those whom He called, these He also justified; and those whom He justified, these He also glorified.

triples.rationale: The burden described across verses 1-2 ends in inability to be saved from war and in captivity. The following address contrasts this with God's own carrying, making and saving of Israel through old age. The reversal of who carries and who can save is explicit in the chapter.

triples.rationale: Both ask to whom the Lord could be likened and immediately contrast Him with human handiwork. Isaiah 40 specifies the craftsman, goldsmith and stabilized wooden image that clarify the kind of comparison being challenged.

Did a craftsman make an image, or did a goldsmith melt gold and gild it, fashioning it as a likeness?

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes measured gold and silver, a hired goldsmith and worship of the handmade result. Jeremiah similarly describes crafted wood adorned with silver and gold and mechanically fastened in place.

triples.rationale: Both passages join God's speaking and bringing the commissioned person with making his journey prosper. Isaiah 46 additionally uses the eastern bird image; that image is not supplied to Isaiah 48.

target_units.text: Rejoice, heavens, because God had mercy on Israel! Sound trumpets, earth’s foundations! Cry out joy, mountains, hills and all their trees! For God redeemed Jacob, and Israel will be glorified.

triples.relationship: lament of being forgotten by God
triples.rationale: Zion says the Lord has forgotten and abandoned her. The psalmist likewise asks how long the Lord will forget him and turn His face away. Both preserve the complaint as the sufferer's speech.
triples.source_text: But Zion said, “The Lord has abandoned me, and the Lord has forgotten me.”

target_units.text: How long, Lord, wilt Thou forget me utterly? How long wilt Thou turn Thy face away from me?

triples.relationship: divine care exceeding parental care
triples.rationale: Isaiah says that even maternal forgetting would not make God forget Zion. The psalm likewise contrasts parental abandonment with the Lord's taking the speaker to Himself. Isaiah poses a maternal possibility; the psalm describes abandonment by both parents.
triples.source_text: “Will a woman forget her child, failing to have mercy on the offspring of her belly? Even if a woman forgets these, I will not forget you,” said the Lord.

target_units.text: For my father and my mother abandoned me, but the Lord took me to Himself.

triples.relationship: internal rebuilding of Zion by unexpected builders
triples.rationale: Isaiah 49 promises rebuilding by those who pulled the city down and departure of its destroyers. Isaiah 60 likewise promises that foreigners will build Zion's walls. Both associate restoration with unexpected human builders, but the passages do not establish that those groups are identical.
triples.source_text: You will swiftly be rebuilt by those who pulled you down, and those who laid you waste will depart from you.

target_units.text: Foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will attend you. For because of My anger I struck you, and because of mercy I loved you.

triples.relationship: internal summons to see gathered children
triples.rationale: Both command Zion to lift her eyes around and see those gathered to her. Isaiah 60 explicitly names sons and daughters; Isaiah 49 pictures the gathered people as her bridal adornment.
triples.source_text: Lift your eyes around and see them all. Behold, they gathered and came to you. As I live, says the Lord, you will put them all on and wrap them around you like a bride’s adornment.

target_units.text: Lift your eyes around you and see your children gathered. Behold, all your sons have come from far away, and your daughters will be lifted upon shoulders.

triples.relationship: bridal adornment as an image of restored joy
triples.rationale: Isaiah 49 compares the gathered people worn by Zion to a bride's adornment. Isaiah 61 likewise compares God-given clothing of salvation and joy to bridal ornaments. The adornment's immediate referent differs.
triples.source_text: Lift your eyes around and see them all. Behold, they gathered and came to you. As I live, says the Lord, you will put them all on and wrap them around you like a bride’s adornment.

target_units.text: and they will rejoice greatly in the Lord.” Let my soul exult in the Lord, for He clothed me in a garment of salvation and a tunic of joy. Like a bridegroom He placed a turban on me, and like a bride He adorned me with ornaments.

triples.relationship: Jerusalem filled again with inhabitants
triples.rationale: Isaiah says formerly ruined places will be cramped with inhabitants. Zechariah likewise promises fruitful habitation of Jerusalem because of the multitude of people and animals, with God protecting the city.
triples.source_text: For your deserted, destroyed, and fallen places will now be cramped by inhabitants, and those swallowing you will be removed far from you.

target_units.text: and said to him, “Run and speak to that young man: Jerusalem will be inhabited fruitfully because of the multitude of people and animals within her.
I will be a wall of fire around her, says the Lord, and I will be glory within her.”

triples.relationship: internal enlargement for unexpectedly numerous children
triples.rationale: The recovered children in Isaiah 49 complain that their dwelling is too cramped. Isaiah 54 answers the corresponding image of the formerly barren woman's numerous children with commands to widen her tent and spread out.
triples.source_text: For your sons whom you lost will say within your hearing, ‘This place is too cramped for me. Make room for me, so I can settle.’

target_units.text: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth! Break out and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the deserted woman’s children are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband,” for the Lord has spoken.
“Widen the place of your tent and your curtains. Pitch them; do not spare! Lengthen your ropes and strengthen your pegs.
Spread out still farther to right and left. Your offspring will inherit nations, and you will settle deserted cities.

triples.relationship: internal astonishment at the deserted mother's children
triples.rationale: Isaiah 49 depicts the childless widow wondering who bore and raised the returning children. Isaiah 54 likewise summons the deserted, non-childbearing woman to rejoice because her children are unexpectedly numerous.
triples.source_text: You will say in your heart, ‘Who bore these for me? I was childless and widowed. Who raised these for me? I was left alone; where were these of mine?’”

target_units.text: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth! Break out and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the deserted woman’s children are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband,” for the Lord has spoken.

triples.relationship: internal return of children carried by others
triples.rationale: Isaiah 49 promises sons brought in bosoms and daughters carried on shoulders. Isaiah 60 repeats the return of sons from afar and daughters lifted upon shoulders, within Zion's gathering.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord: “Behold, I lift My hand toward nations and will raise My signal toward islands. They will bring your sons in their bosom and carry your daughters on shoulders,

target_units.text: Lift your eyes around you and see your children gathered. Behold, all your sons have come from far away, and your daughters will be lifted upon shoulders.

triples.relationship: royal bowing and dust imagery
triples.rationale: Isaiah pictures rulers bowing to Zion and licking the dust of her feet. The psalm likewise joins kings bowing with enemies licking dust. The groups assigned the dust-licking action differ, while the homage imagery is shared.
triples.source_text: and kings will be your foster fathers and ruling women your nurses. They will bow to you upon the earth’s surface and lick the dust of your feet. You will know that I am the Lord, and you will not be ashamed.

target_units.text: Ethiopians will fall before him, and his enemies will lick dust.
kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; kings of the Arabians and Saba will bring gifts.
And all kings will bow before him; all nations will serve him.

triples.relationship: strong man's possessions and the question of plunder
triples.rationale: Isaiah asks whether spoils can be taken from a giant. Jesus similarly asks how someone can seize the strong man's possessions without first binding him. The comparison concerns the obstacle to rescue or plunder; Matthew applies it to His work against demons.
triples.source_text: Will anyone take spoils from a giant? If someone takes captives unjustly, will he be saved?”

target_units.text: But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
Or how can someone enter the strong man’s house and seize his belongings unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.

triples.relationship: victory over the strong and taking spoils
triples.rationale: Isaiah connects taking from a strong man with rescue and God's judgment for His people's sons. Luke likewise describes a stronger attacker defeating an armed strong man and distributing his spoils. Luke's setting does not identify the captives named by Isaiah.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord: “If someone captures a giant, he will take spoils; one taking from a strong man will be saved. I will judge your case, and I will rescue your sons.

target_units.text: When the strong man, fully armed, guards his own courtyard, his possessions are at peace.
But when someone stronger than he attacks and defeats him, he takes away the full armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils.

triples.relationship: internal recognition of the saving God after reversal
triples.rationale: Both culminate in recognition that the Lord saves or rescues His people. Isaiah 49 reaches that confession through the afflicters' destruction; Isaiah 60 reaches it through the nations' provision and royal wealth. The connection does not transfer self-consuming violence to Isaiah 60.
triples.source_text: Those who afflicted you will eat their own flesh, drink their own blood like new wine, and become drunk. All flesh will perceive that I am the Lord who rescued you and upholds Jacob’s strength.”

target_units.text: You will suck the nations’ milk and eat kings’ wealth. You will know that I am the Lord who saves and delivers you, Israel’s God.

triples.relationship: divorce imagery for a people's unfaithfulness
triples.rationale: Isaiah asks for the mother's divorce document and explains the sending away through lawless acts. Jeremiah expressly describes Israel receiving a divorce certificate after unfaithfulness. Isaiah's question and its term debtor remain distinct from Jeremiah's narrative.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord: “What is your mother’s divorce document with which I sent her away? Or to which debtor have I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and I sent your mother away because of your lawless acts.

target_units.text: The Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah, You saw what the dwelling of Israel did to Me. They went upon every high mountain and beneath every wooded tree and prostituted themselves there.
After she prostituted herself in all these ways, I said, Return to Me. But she did not return, and faithless Judah saw her faithlessness.

I saw that, concerning all the things in which the dwelling of Israel was caught committing adultery, I sent her away and gave a certificate of divorce into her hands. Yet faithless Judah did not fear; she too went and prostituted herself.

triples.relationship: internal question about the Lord's saving hand
triples.rationale: Both ask whether God's hand lacks power to save. Isaiah 59 answers by locating separation in the people's offenses; Isaiah 50 likewise surrounds the question with sin, failed response and demonstrations of God's power.
triples.source_text: Why did I come when no person was there, call when no one obeyed? Is My hand not strong enough to rescue? Am I not able to deliver? Behold, by My threat I will make the sea desolate and turn rivers to deserts; their fish will dry up for lack of water and die in thirst.

target_units.text: Is the Lord’s hand unable to save? Or has His ear grown heavy so that He cannot hear?
Instead, your offenses stand between you and God, and because of your sins He has turned His face away from you so as not to show mercy.

triples.relationship: divine judgment leaving a river's fish dead
triples.rationale: Isaiah describes waters made dry and fish dying for lack of water. Exodus narrates fish dying when the river becomes blood. The common feature is God's judgment on water with dead fish; the mechanism differs and is not harmonized.
triples.source_text: Why did I come when no person was there, call when no one obeyed? Is My hand not strong enough to rescue? Am I not able to deliver? Behold, by My threat I will make the sea desolate and turn rivers to deserts; their fish will dry up for lack of water and die in thirst.

target_units.text: Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded. He raised his staff and struck the river’s water before Pharaoh and his attendants, and all the water in the river turned to blood.
The fish in the river died, and the river stank. The Egyptians could not drink its water, and there was blood throughout the land of Egypt.

triples.relationship: divinely imposed darkness
triples.rationale: Isaiah says God clothes heaven in darkness like sackcloth. Exodus narrates His command for darkness over Egypt. The narrative supplies a concrete counterpart to imposed darkness, without supplying Isaiah's clothing metaphor.
triples.source_text: I will clothe heaven in darkness and make its covering like sackcloth.”

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness upon the land of Egypt, darkness that may be felt.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

triples.relationship: instruction attributed to the One who sends
triples.rationale: Isaiah's speaker attributes the instructed tongue and listening ear to the Lord. Jesus likewise attributes His teaching to the One who sent Him when hearers question its source. Neither comparison adds a reference to the weary that is absent from Isaiah's supplied wording.
triples.source_text: The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know the right time when a word must be spoken. He appointed morning for me; He added an ear for me to hear,

So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not Mine, but belongs to the One who sent Me.

triples.relationship: obedient response to divine instruction
triples.rationale: Isaiah's speaker says the Lord's instruction opens his ears and he does not disobey. Jesus similarly says He always does what pleases the One who sent Him. Both state the speaker's obedience, in different settings.
triples.source_text: and the Lord’s instruction opens my ears. I do not disobey or contradict.

target_units.text: And the One who sent Me is with Me. He has not left Me alone, because I always do the things pleasing to Him.”

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes offering cheeks to slaps and not turning the face from spitting. Matthew narrates people spitting into Jesus's face, striking and slapping Him. These particular acts supply the narrative parallel.

triples.relationship: firmly setting the face toward an ordeal
triples.rationale: Isaiah's speaker sets his face like solid rock in confidence in God's help. Luke describes Jesus firmly setting His face toward Jerusalem as His being taken up approaches. The shared expression depicts determination; Luke does not repeat the rock comparison.

target_units.text: As the days for His being taken up approached their fulfillment, He firmly set His face to go to Jerusalem.

triples.rationale: Isaiah pairs the nearness of the One justifying with repeated challenges to anyone bringing a case. Romans likewise asks who can bring a charge or condemn when God justifies, then names Christ's death, resurrection and intercession.

triples.relationship: divine instruction held within the heart
triples.rationale: Isaiah identifies the addressed people as having God's law in their heart. The psalmist likewise places God's sayings in his heart so that he may avoid sinning. This connects the inward instruction clause rather than the distinct reproach clause.
triples.source_text: Listen to Me, you who know judgment, My people with My law in your heart. Do not fear people’s reproach or be overcome by their contempt.

triples.relationship: internal recurrence of the moth-eaten garment
triples.rationale: Both use the aging garment and consuming moth for what cannot endure. Isaiah 51 expressly contrasts such decay with God's everlasting righteousness and salvation; Isaiah 50 applies the decay to opponents.
triples.source_text: For a garment will be consumed by time, and wool eaten by a moth. But My righteousness will last for ever, and My salvation through generations of generations.”

triples.rationale: Both summon Jerusalem or Zion to awake and clothe herself with strength. The addressee in Isaiah 51 is Jerusalem, and the comparison does not introduce a dragon or Rahab absent from its actual wording.

triples.source_text: and ransomed? For by the Lord they will be brought back and come to Zion with joy and everlasting exultation. Exultation and praise are upon their heads; joy will overtake them. Pain, sorrow, and sighing fled.

triples.rationale: Jerusalem has drunk the cup and bowl of anger in Isaiah. Jeremiah receives a cup from the Lord's hand for the nations, whose drinking brings madness before the sword. The shared cup is an image of imposed judgment.

triples.rationale: Both describe the daughter's crushing and ask who will comfort her. Lamentations also depicts children failing for want of food, corresponding to Isaiah's named famine and destruction.

triples.relationship: helpless children in the city's public places

triples.source_text: Your sons are helpless, sleeping at every way out like a half-boiled beet, full of the Lord’s anger, exhausted because of the Lord God.

target_units.text: My eyes failed with tears; my heart was troubled. My glory was poured onto the ground at the shattering of the daughter of my people, as infant and nursing child failed in the city’s squares.

triples.relationship: internal drunkenness without wine
triples.rationale: Both explicitly describe a disordered, weakened condition as drunkenness or hangover without wine. Isaiah 51 places that description in the context of the cup of divine anger.
triples.source_text: Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.

target_units.text: Grow faint, lose your senses and suffer a hangover, neither from sikera nor from wine,

triples.relationship: end of Zion's punishment and transfer of the cup

triples.relationship: oppressors receiving the cup after Zion
triples.rationale: Isaiah transfers the cup to those who humiliated Jerusalem. Lamentations likewise announces the cup's arrival at Edom while Zion's deportation ends. Isaiah's account of the bowed back as a walkway remains its own description of abuse.
triples.source_text: I will throw it into the hands of those who wronged and humbled you, who told your soul, “Bend down, so we may pass.” You laid your back level with the earth, outside for passersby.’”

target_units.text: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Idumea, dwelling upon the land! To you too the Lord’s cup will pass; you will become drunk and pour it out.

triples.relationship: holiness of Jerusalem and restricted entry
triples.rationale: Isaiah calls Jerusalem the holy city and promises that uncircumcised and unclean people will no longer pass through her. Joel likewise calls Jerusalem holy and says foreigners will no longer pass through; the excluded groups are named differently.
triples.source_text: Awake, awake, Zion! Clothe yourself with your strength, Zion, and put on your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. No uncircumcised and unclean person will pass through you again.

target_units.text: You will recognize that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion on My holy mountain. Jerusalem will be a holy city, and foreigners will no longer pass through her.

triples.relationship: internal release and reversal of Zion's humiliation
triples.rationale: Isaiah commands captive daughter Zion to rise from dust and remove her neck bond. Isaiah 61 announces release for captives and glory and joy in place of mourning for Zion. The target does not specifically repeat the neck bond.
triples.source_text: Shake off the dust and rise; sit, Jerusalem. Strip off the bond around your neck, captive daughter Zion.

target_units.text: The Lord’s spirit is upon me, because He anointed me. He sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind,
to announce the Lord’s acceptable year and a day of recompense, to comfort all who mourn,

so that Zion’s mourners may receive glory instead of ashes, an ointment of joy for those who mourn, a robe of glory instead of a spirit of despondency. They will be called Generations of Righteousness, the Lord’s planting, for glory.

triples.relationship: ransom distinguished from payment in silver
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises ransom without silver after being sold for nothing. Peter likewise says redemption was not with perishable silver or gold, then names Christ's precious blood. The target supplies its own positive account of redemption's means.
triples.source_text: For thus says the Lord: “You were sold for nothing, and without silver you will be ransomed.”

target_units.text: knowing that you were ransomed from the futile conduct handed down from your ancestors, not with perishable things, silver or gold,
but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot—the blood of Christ,

triples.relationship: narrative counterpart to Israel's descent into Egypt
triples.rationale: Isaiah recalls the people's earlier migration to Egypt. Genesis narrates Jacob's household and possessions entering Egypt, naming the children and descendants who went with him.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord: “My people formerly went down to Egypt to live there as strangers, and they were forcibly led to the Assyrians.

target_units.text: And Jacob rose from the Well of the Oath; and the sons of Israel carried their father and their households and their wives upon the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him.

his sons and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters and his sons’ daughters; and all his seed he brought into Egypt.

triples.relationship: narrative counterpart to deportation to Assyria
triples.rationale: Isaiah pairs the earlier stay in Egypt with forcible removal to the Assyrians. Kings records the Assyrian king's capture of Samaria and deportation of Israel, with the places of resettlement.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord: “My people formerly went down to Egypt to live there as strangers, and they were forcibly led to the Assyrians.

triples.relationship: explicit citation of God's name blasphemed
triples.rationale: Romans introduces as written the saying that God's name is blasphemed among the nations because of the addressed people. Isaiah contains that same accusation within its lament over the people's captivity.
triples.source_text: And now, why are you here?” Thus says the Lord. “My people were taken for nothing. Be amazed and wail!” Thus says the Lord. “Because of you, My name is continually blasphemed among the nations.

target_units.text: For “the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you,” just as it is written.

triples.relationship: recognition of the Lord through His promised rescue
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises that His people will know His name as the One who speaks and is present. Exodus likewise joins the declaration I am the Lord with rescue and the promise that Israel will know Him as their delivering God.
triples.source_text: Therefore My people will know My name on that day, because I am the One speaking. I am present

target_units.text: Go, say to the sons of Israel: ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the Egyptians’ domination and deliver you from slavery. I will ransom you with an uplifted arm and with great judgment.
And I will take you to Myself for a people, and I will be your God; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the oppression of the Egyptians.

triples.relationship: explicit reuse of the good-news messenger's feet
triples.rationale: Romans introduces a scriptural saying about the beautiful feet of those announcing good things within its argument for sent proclaimers. triples.relationship: close prophetic messenger parallel
triples.rationale: Both bring together mountains, the feet of a good-news bearer and the announcement of peace. Nahum directs Judah to celebrate after the hostile passage has ended; Isaiah announces salvation and God's reign to Zion.

triples.relationship: internal voices of Jerusalem's appointed guards
triples.rationale: Isaiah 52 describes the city's guards raising their voices together at the Lord's mercy. Isaiah 62 likewise appoints guards upon Jerusalem's walls who will not be silent as they remember the Lord, in the context of restoration.
triples.source_text: For the voice of those guarding you was raised, and together they will rejoice with their voice. For eyes will see eye to eye when the Lord has mercy on Zion.

target_units.text: Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I appointed guards all day and all night, who will never be silent as they remember the Lord.

triples.relationship: internal joy of restored deserted places
triples.rationale: Both call attention to Zion or Jerusalem's deserted places receiving divine mercy and renewed joy. Isaiah 51 adds the paradise comparison and thanksgiving; Isaiah 52 specifically names Jerusalem's rescue.
triples.source_text: Let Jerusalem’s deserted places break out in joy together, for the Lord had mercy on her and rescued Jerusalem.

target_units.text: I will now comfort you, Zion; I have comforted all her deserted places and will make her deserted places like the Lord’s paradise. They will find joy and exultation in her, thanksgiving and a voice of praise.

triples.relationship: God's salvation seen at the ends of earth
triples.rationale: Both announce salvation made visible before nations and seen by all earth's ends. The psalm joins that worldwide recognition with remembered mercy to Jacob and Israel.
triples.source_text: The Lord will uncover His holy arm before all nations, and all the ends of earth will see the salvation that comes from God.

target_units.text: The Lord made His salvation known; before the nations He revealed His righteousness.
He remembered His mercy to Jacob and His truth to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God.

triples.relationship: scriptural reuse of departure and separation from uncleanness
triples.rationale: Paul repeats the command to come out, be separated and touch nothing unclean in his address to believers as God's temple. Isaiah addresses those carrying the Lord's vessels; that immediate temple-service setting is not erased.
triples.source_text: Depart, depart; go out from there, and do not touch anything unclean. Go out from her midst; separate yourselves, you who carry the Lord’s vessels.

target_units.text: And what agreement is there between God’s temple and idols? For we are the temple of the living God, just as God said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.

triples.relationship: God leading the departing people
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises that the Lord will go ahead of His people as they depart without turmoil or flight. Exodus narrates God leading the people with the cloud and fire before them. Isaiah's supplied final description names the One gathering them, not a rearguard.
triples.source_text: For you will not go out in turmoil or travel in flight, because the Lord will go ahead of you, and the One gathering you is the Lord, Israel’s God.

target_units.text: God led them by day in a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not cease before all the people.

triples.relationship: servant status followed by divine exaltation
triples.rationale: Isaiah announces the servant's exaltation and great glory. Philippians likewise joins Christ's taking a slave's form and humbling Himself with God's highly exalting Him. The comparison does not claim Isaiah states every stage of Paul's account.
triples.source_text: Behold, My servant will understand, and will be exalted and greatly glorified.

target_units.text: but emptied Himself, taking the form of a slave, coming to be in the likeness of human beings; and being found in appearance as a human being,

so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth,
and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

triples.relationship: internal repeated description of dishonored appearance
triples.rationale: The servant's form and glory without honor in Isaiah 52 recur in Isaiah 53's absence of form, beauty and honor and the sufferer's being held of no account. The continuation develops the same portrait.
triples.source_text: As many will be astonished at you— so your form will be without honour among men, and your glory among men—

triples.relationship: explicit citation about previously unreached hearers
triples.rationale: Paul quotes the seeing of those not previously told and the understanding of those who have not heard, corresponding to Isaiah's final clause. He applies it to proclaiming Christ where He has not been named; Isaiah also describes the nations' wonder and kings' silence.
triples.source_text: so many nations will marvel at him, and kings will close their mouths. For those to whom he was not proclaimed will see, and those who have not heard will understand.

target_units.text: and so making it my ambition to proclaim the gospel where Christ has not been named, so that I would not build on another’s foundation,
but just as it is written, “Those to whom nothing about Him was announced will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

triples.relationship: explicit quotation attributed to Isaiah
triples.rationale: John explicitly names Isaiah and quotes both the question about believing the report and the question about the revealed arm of the Lord. He applies the saying to unbelief despite Jesus's signs.

so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke: “Lord, who believed our report? And to whom was the arm of the Lord revealed?”

Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory and spoke concerning Him.

triples.relationship: explicit quotation concerning the received report
triples.rationale: Paul names Isaiah and repeats the question about who believed the report in his discussion of hearing and obedience to the gospel. This corresponds to the first question of the source verse.
triples.source_text: O Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?

target_units.text: But not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who believed our report?”

triples.rationale: Isaiah 53 says the figure has no form, glory or beauty; Isaiah 52 already describes the form and glory as without honor among people. The connection concerns that repeated description and leaves the unusual opening We proclaimed before him as a child intact.

triples.rationale: Isaiah describes an afflicted figure dishonored and held of no account. The psalm likewise presents a sufferer as an object of human reproach and contempt, mocked by onlookers. Its mockery is not converted into Isaiah's explicit sickness language.

triples.rationale: Isaiah expressly says the figure bears our sins and suffers pain for us. Peter likewise says Christ suffered for the addressed people and bore their sins in His body. The connection follows the actual sin-bearing wording.

triples.source_text: from the toil of his soul, to show him light and fashion him with understanding, to justify the righteous one who serves many well; and he will bear their sins.

triples.source_text: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth! Break out and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the deserted woman’s children are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband,” for the Lord has spoken.

triples.rationale: Isaiah promises offspring inheriting nations and settling deserted cities. Genesis likewise promises Abraham's multiplied seed inheritance of adversaries' cities. The nations and the deserted condition are Isaiah's particular formulations.
triples.source_text: Spread out still farther to right and left. Your offspring will inherit nations, and you will settle deserted cities.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 54 promises that widowhood's reproach will be forgotten and shame need not cause fear. Isaiah 49 likewise moves from Zion's memory of being childless and widowed to returned children, royal service and the assurance that she will not be ashamed.
triples.source_text: Do not fear because you were put to shame, or be abashed because you were reproached. For you will forget lasting shame and never remember the reproach of your widowhood.

triples.source_text: “The Lord has not called you like an abandoned, fainthearted wife, nor like a wife hated since youth,” says your God.

triples.rationale: Isaiah 54 contrasts a short abandonment with great mercy. Isaiah 60 likewise explains the city's restoration by contrasting God's anger in striking with His mercy in loving.

triples.rationale: Isaiah contrasts little anger and a turned face with everlasting mercy. Micah likewise says God does not retain anger because He desires mercy, and recalls His sworn mercy to the ancestors.

triples.source_text: “This dates for Me from the water in Noah’s time, when I swore to him then concerning the earth not to be angry with you again, nor at a threat against you

target_units.text: And God spoke to Noah and to his sons with him, saying,
“Behold, I establish My covenant with you and with your seed after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the cattle, and all the wild beasts of the earth with you, all that came out of the ark.
“And I will establish My covenant with you: never again shall all flesh perish by the waters of a flood, and never again shall there be a flood of water to destroy the whole earth.”
And the Lord God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant which I give between Me and you and every living creature with you, for everlasting generations:
I set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.
“And when I gather clouds over the earth, My bow shall appear in the cloud.
And I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall never again become a flood to blot out all flesh.
“My bow shall be in the cloud, and I will look upon it and remember the everlasting covenant between Me and every living creature of all flesh upon the earth.”
And God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant which I have established between Me and all flesh upon the earth.”

triples.relationship: unremoved and everlasting covenant of peace
triples.rationale: Isaiah says the covenant of peace will never be removed and mercy will not fail. Ezekiel likewise promises a covenant of peace explicitly called everlasting. Isaiah's assurance about mountains and hills is preserved without converting it into their removal.
triples.source_text: for mountains to move away; nor will your hills be shifted. So neither will My mercy toward you fail, nor will your covenant of peace ever be removed.” For the Lord said, “I am gracious to you.”

target_units.text: I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant with them. I will set My holy things among them for ever.

triples.relationship: explicit prophetic citation of divine teaching
triples.rationale: Jesus introduces as written in the Prophets the saying that all will be taught by God, corresponding to Isaiah's description of the sons. He applies hearing and learning from the Father to coming to Him.
triples.source_text: and all your sons taught by God, and your children in great peace.

target_units.text: No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day.
It is written in the Prophets, ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to Me.

triples.relationship: internal restoration of Zion in righteousness
triples.rationale: Isaiah 54 promises a city built in righteousness and calls for separation from injustice. Isaiah 1 likewise promises restored judges and the name City of Righteousness, joining Zion's salvation with judgment and mercy.
triples.source_text: You will be built in righteousness. Keep away from injustice, and you will not fear; terror will not approach you.

target_units.text: I will establish your judges as before and your counselors as at the beginning. After these things you will be called City of Righteousness, Faithful Metropolis Zion.
For her captivity will be saved through judgment and through mercy.

triples.relationship: nations taking refuge with the restored people
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises newcomers approaching through God and taking refuge with the addressed city. Zechariah likewise says many nations will take refuge with the Lord, become His people and dwell within Zion. The native Isaiah wording is positive arrival, not hostile gathering.
triples.source_text: Behold, newcomers will approach you through Me and take refuge with you.

target_units.text: “Delight and rejoice, daughter Zion, for look, I am coming and will dwell within you,” says the Lord.
Many nations will take refuge with the Lord on that day and become His people. They will dwell within you, and you will recognize that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you.

triples.relationship: creation's purpose distinguished from destruction
triples.rationale: Isaiah says God is creating the addressed people and did not create them for ruin. Wisdom likewise denies that God made death or delights in destruction and says He created things to exist. Isaiah's contrast with a smith remains distinct from this broader account of creation.
triples.source_text: Behold, I am creating you, not like a smith blowing coals and bringing out an implement for work. I did not create you for ruin, to destroy

target_units.text: For God did not make death, neither does He delight in the destruction of the living.
For He created all things that they might exist, and the created things of the world are life-preserving; there is no poison of destruction in them, nor is Hades’ dominion upon the earth.

triples.relationship: divine vindication against hostile legal claims
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises defeat of voices raised against the addressed people in judgment and righteousness before God for His servants. Romans similarly asks who can bring a charge or condemn when God justifies. The legal vindication is shared without importing the source's implements into Romans.
triples.source_text: every perishable implement. I will not grant success against you. Every voice will rise against you in judgment; you will defeat them all, and those accountable to you will be held liable in it. There is an inheritance for those serving the Lord, and you will be righteous before Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: What, then, shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?
He who did not spare His own Son, but handed Him over for us all, how will He not also graciously give us all things with Him?
Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? God is the One who justifies.
Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is the One who died—more than that, was raised—who is also at God’s right hand, who also intercedes for us.

triples.relationship: invitation to the thirsty to come and drink
triples.rationale: Isaiah calls the thirsty to water and offers drink without price. Jesus likewise calls anyone thirsty to come to Him and drink; John explains the saying with reference to the Spirit. The source's wine and rich food remain its own features.
triples.source_text: You who thirst, go to the water; and you who have no silver, go and buy wine and rich food, and drink without silver or price.

target_units.text: On the last day, the great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink.
The one who believes in Me—as the Scripture said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”
He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were about to receive; for the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

triples.relationship: life-giving water offered as a gift
triples.rationale: Isaiah invites those without money to receive water and drink without price. Jesus describes God's gift of living water which He gives and which becomes a spring into eternal life. The connection is the offered sustaining gift, not an identification of ordinary purchased water.
triples.source_text: You who thirst, go to the water; and you who have no silver, go and buy wine and rich food, and drink without silver or price.

target_units.text: Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God and who it is who says to you, ‘Give Me a drink,’ you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.”
The woman said to Him, “Sir, Thou hast no vessel for drawing water, and the well is deep. Where, then, dost Thou get this living water?
Art Thou greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, and his sons and his livestock?”
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again.
But whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will certainly never thirst; rather, the water I will give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.”

triples.relationship: labor redirected from inadequate food to lasting provision
triples.rationale: Isaiah questions spending money and toil on what fails to satisfy and calls the people to listen and eat good things. Jesus likewise redirects labor from perishing food to the food enduring to eternal life which He gives.
triples.source_text: Why do you pay a price of silver, and give your toil for what does not satisfy? Listen to Me, and you will eat good things, and your soul will delight in good things.

target_units.text: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for upon Him the Father, God, has set His seal.”

triples.relationship: explicit citation of David's holy and sure blessings
triples.rationale: Acts quotes the holy and sure blessings of David within the proclamation of Jesus's resurrection and the fulfilled ancestral promise. Isaiah names those blessings within God's offer of an everlasting covenant.
triples.source_text: Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.

target_units.text: We proclaim to you the good news of the promise made to the fathers:
God has fulfilled this for us, their children, by raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: ‘Thou art My Son; today I have begotten Thee.’
God has spoken this way about raising Him from the dead, never again to return to decay: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’
Therefore He also says in another place, ‘Thou wilt not allow Thy Holy One to see decay.’
For David, after serving his own generation according to God’s purpose, fell asleep, was gathered to his fathers, and saw decay.
But the One whom God raised did not see decay.

triples.relationship: covenant sworn to David with enduring offspring
triples.rationale: Isaiah associates the everlasting covenant with David's sure blessings. The psalm explicitly describes God's covenant and oath to David, promising his offspring and throne through generations.
triples.source_text: Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.

target_units.text: “I made a covenant with My chosen ones; I swore to David My servant:
‘I will prepare your seed for ever and build your throne from generation to generation.’” Diapsalma.

triples.relationship: royal appointment over nations
triples.rationale: Isaiah speaks of a figure given as ruler and commander of nations following the Davidic blessings. David's song likewise credits God with preserving him as head of nations. The comparison concerns the royal commission without resolving every referent of Isaiah's him.
triples.source_text: Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a ruler and commander of nations.

target_units.text: Thou wilt rescue me from the battle of peoples; Thou wilt preserve me as head of nations. A people I did not know served me.

triples.relationship: response of previously unknown peoples
triples.rationale: Isaiah promises that nations formerly unacquainted with the addressed figure will call and seek refuge. David's song likewise speaks of a people he did not know serving him and foreigners obeying as soon as they hear. The responses are related but not identical.
triples.source_text: Nations that did not know you will call upon you, and peoples that do not know you will flee to you for refuge, because of your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you.

target_units.text: Thou wilt rescue me from the battle of peoples; Thou wilt preserve me as head of nations. A people I did not know served me.
Foreigners lied to me; as soon as their ears heard, they obeyed me.

triples.relationship: seeking, finding and returning to God
triples.rationale: Isaiah commands seeking God and calling when He is found; the following clause joins His drawing near with the call to return. Deuteronomy likewise promises that the people will seek and find the Lord with their whole heart and return to His voice. Isaiah's wording is not changed to while He may be found.
triples.source_text: Seek God, and when you find Him, call upon Him; and when He draws near to you,

target_units.text: And there you shall seek the Lord your God, and shall find Him, when you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul, in your distress.
And all these things shall find you in the latter days, and you shall return unto the Lord your God, and hearken unto His voice.
For the Lord your God is a merciful God; He will not forsake you, neither will He destroy you, nor forget the covenant of your fathers which He sware unto them.

triples.relationship: turning from lawlessness and receiving mercy
triples.rationale: Isaiah calls the lawless to abandon their ways and counsels, return and receive abundant forgiveness. Ezekiel similarly promises life and non-remembrance of transgressions when the lawless turn from their deeds and practice righteousness and mercy.
triples.source_text: let the ungodly forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels; and let him return to the Lord, and he will receive mercy; for He will abundantly forgive your sins.

target_units.text: If the lawless person turns from all the lawlessness he committed, keeps all My commandments, and practices righteousness and mercy, he will surely live; he certainly will not die.
None of the transgressions he committed will be remembered. By the righteousness he practiced, he will live.
Do I at all desire the death of the lawless, says the Lord, rather than his turning from his evil way and living?

triples.relationship: divine ways and counsel beyond human understanding
triples.rationale: Isaiah distinguishes God's counsels and ways from those of the hearers. Romans likewise calls His ways untraceable and asks who has known His mind or served as His counselor. It is a conceptual parallel, not an assertion that Romans cites this verse verbatim.
triples.source_text: For My counsels are not as your counsels, nor are My ways like your ways, says the Lord.

target_units.text: O depth of God’s wealth and wisdom and knowledge! How unsearchable His judgments and untraceable His ways!
“For who knew the Lord’s mind? Or who became His counselor?
Or who gave to Him first, and it will be repaid to him?”
Because from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory throughout the ages. Amen.

triples.relationship: heaven's height above earth as a measure of divine greatness
triples.rationale: Isaiah uses the distance of heaven from earth to compare God's ways and thoughts with human ones. The psalm uses the same vertical comparison for God's mercy toward those fearing Him. The measured divine qualities differ.
triples.source_text: But as the heaven is distant from the earth, so is My way distant from your ways, and your thoughts from My mind.

target_units.text: for according to heaven’s height above the earth, the Lord strengthened His mercy toward those who fear Him.

triples.relationship: reuse of seed for the sower and bread for food
triples.rationale: Isaiah describes rain's fruitful result as seed for the sower and bread for food. Paul repeats that paired provision in naming God as supplier and adds multiplication of the readers' seed and fruits of righteousness.
triples.source_text: For as rain or snow comes down from the heaven, and does not return until it has drenched the earth, and made it bring forth and sprout, and given seed to the sower and bread for food,

target_units.text: Now the One who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness.

triples.relationship: divine speech accomplished in action
triples.rationale: Isaiah says the word from God's mouth will accomplish His will before returning. Numbers likewise asks whether God would speak and not act or abide by His speech, distinguishing His reliability from human weakness.
triples.source_text: so it will be with My word, whatever goes out from My mouth: it will certainly not return until all that I have willed is accomplished; and I will prosper your ways and My commandments.

target_units.text: God is not as a man, to be led astray, nor as a son of man, to be threatened; having spoken, shall He not act? Shall He speak, and not abide by it?

triples.relationship: nature personified in joyful response
triples.rationale: Isaiah pictures mountains and hills welcoming with joy and trees clapping branches. The psalm likewise makes rivers clap and mountains exult at God's coming. The images support the connection without changing Isaiah's being taught in joy into being led.
triples.source_text: For you will go out in gladness, and in joy you will be taught; for the mountains and the hills will leap, welcoming you with joy, and all the trees of the field will clap their branches.

target_units.text: Let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it, the inhabited world and those who dwell in it.
Rivers will clap their hands together; the mountains will exult,
for He has come to judge the earth. He will judge the inhabited world with righteousness and peoples with uprightness.

triples.relationship: internal planting of named trees displaying God's work
triples.rationale: Isaiah 55 replaces thorny growth with cypress and myrtle and says the Lord will be for a name and an everlasting sign. Isaiah 41 likewise places cypress and myrtle among trees in formerly waterless land so that people recognize the Lord's action.
triples.source_text: And the cypress will rise in place of the thorny shrub, and the myrtle will rise in place of the fleabane; and the Lord will be for a name and for an everlasting sign, and will not fail.

target_units.text: but will open rivers on mountains and springs amid plains. I will make the wilderness marshes and the thirsty land watercourses,
and will place cedar, box tree, myrtle, cypress, and white poplar in the waterless land,
so that they may see and know, consider and understand together that the Lord’s hand did all these things and Israel’s Holy One displayed them.

deferred_source_units.reason: The battlements of jasper, crystal-stone gates and enclosing choice-stone wall remain an exact-text pending unit. The Revelation lead is unread because the pinned record is unavailable; no alternate gemstone or architecture wording was substituted.

target_units.text: When evening came, they brought Him many who were oppressed by demons. He cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were ill,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “He took our weaknesses and carried our diseases.”

unresolved_candidates.reason: Matthew explicitly attributes the saying about taking weaknesses and carrying diseases to Isaiah, whereas the supplied Isaiah verse says he bears our sins and suffers pain for us. A proposed exact-wording equivalence is not retained; the direct sin-bearing counterpart in 1 Peter is separately supported. unresolved_candidates.source_text: And I will give the wicked in exchange for his burial, and the rich in exchange for his death; for he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

target_units.text: When evening came, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph came, who himself had also become Jesus’ disciple.
He went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. Then Pilate ordered it to be given.
Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.
He laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. Rolling a great stone to the tomb’s entrance, he went away.

unresolved_candidates.reason: Matthew narrates rich Joseph placing Jesus's body in his tomb.
